records.title: Share Price Versus Company Size — Mega-Cap Example
records.claim: Share price alone cannot identify total issuer size.
records.worked: FICTIONAL 100 million shares × $10 = $1 billion market cap.
records.counterexample: A company trading at $500 with only 100,000 shares has $50 million capitalization, not more than $1 billion.
records.transfer: Compute 40 million shares × $8; explain why $320 million is not corporate cash.

records.title: ETF Versus Index
records.claim: An index measures a basket; an ETF is a separately traded fund.
records.worked: FICTIONAL: index 100 to 102 represents 2% index change, not guaranteed matching ETF return.
records.counterexample: A market index value is not directly a tradable security; ETF shares incur trading spreads and costs.
records.transfer: Name differences among an ETF's NAV, market price, benchmark and the fund's prospectus.

records.title: Bid, Ask, Last, Spread, and Midpoint in a Frequently Updating Quote
records.claim: Bid, ask, last transaction, midpoint and spread describe distinct measurements.
records.worked: FICTIONAL bid $10.00, ask $10.08, last $10.03: spread=$0.08; midpoint=$10.04.
records.counterexample: Neither midpoint nor last trade is a guaranteed price for a new order.
records.transfer: Recalculate bid $19.95, ask $20.10: spread=$0.15 and midpoint=$20.025; discuss missing size.

records.title: Compare Quote Width Without Jumping Ahead to Liquidity Analysis
records.claim: Spread width is not by itself reliable evidence of executable depth.
records.worked: FICTIONAL spreads: $20.00/$20.05 has $0.05 width; $20.00/$20.30 has $0.30 width.
records.counterexample: A narrow spread for ten displayed shares cannot guarantee a 1,000-share fill.
records.transfer: Compare $8.40/$8.48 with $8.40/$8.56 and name unknown size, time and venue.

records.title: Order Selection, Fills, Partial Fills, and Execution Control — Market Orders
records.claim: A market order does not guarantee the last reported execution price.
records.worked: FICTIONAL: buy 100 shares when displayed ask is $5.08 with only 20 shares; full fill at $5.08 is unproven.
records.counterexample: A past $5.00 last trade cannot promise the next 100-share buy at $5.00.
records.transfer: Describe the actual order confirmation, clock, route and size needed to verify a fill.

records.title: Order Selection, Fills, Partial Fills, and Execution Control — Marketable Limit Orders
records.claim: Buy limits constrain price but do not guarantee order execution.
records.worked: FICTIONAL 100-share buy limit $5.06 sees 30 offered shares at $5.06; the rest might not fill.
records.counterexample: Merely touching a buy limit in past prices does not establish that the whole order executed.
records.transfer: Compare a $6.10 buy limit against an ask of $6.08 with 10 shown shares for a 100-share order.

records.title: Stops and Invalidation — Slippage and gaps
records.claim: Stop trigger is not the guaranteed exit price.
records.worked: FICTIONAL entry $10.00, stop $9.80; 100 shares filled on exit at $9.50 lose $50, not the planned $20.
records.counterexample: Confusing a planned stop with an enforceable loss ceiling hides gap and slippage risks.
records.transfer: At $10 entry and $9.40 exit, compute 80-share loss $48, then explain the stop-price caveat.

records.title: VWAP and Moving Averages in Intraday Trading — VWAP as a session reference
records.claim: VWAP requires defined bar/tick input scope and session boundary.
records.worked: FICTIONAL HLC3 bar proxy: $9.50 at volume 100 and $10.50 at volume 200 gives (950+2100)/300=$10.1667.
records.counterexample: A bar typical-price proxy is not a tick-accurate VWAP or buy signal.
records.transfer: Use two fresh fictional bar prices $10 at 100 units and $12 at 300 units; calculate $11.50 proxy.
